title: Big Tech's AI Spending Spree Is Eating Into Free Cash Flow, and Investors Are Worried
excerpt: A Reuters analysis shows hyperscalers will spend $1.57 for every $1 of additional cash flow by 2027, as Alphabet kicks off a pivotal earnings season on Wednesday.
body:
The five companies that have powered Wall Street's AI rally are running into a problem: they are spending money faster than they are making it.

Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle — the so-called hyperscalers — are expected to spend more combined on capital expenditures than they generate in free cash flow by 2027, according to a Reuters analysis of LSEG consensus estimates published Tuesday. The data shows these companies will produce about $340 billion more in annual operating cash flow in 2027 compared with 2025, but capex is projected to rise by roughly $534 billion over the same period — the equivalent of $1.57 in new investment for every $1 of additional cash flow.

"Investors are underestimating how fundamentally AI is changing the Big Tech business model. These companies were historically valued as asset-light platforms because revenue could scale much faster than capital requirements, but AI is pushing them toward a hybrid model where software, advertising and cloud economics increasingly depend on enormous physical infrastructure spending."

— Shay Boloor, Chief Market Strategist, Futurum Equities

The Numbers Behind the Squeeze

The scale of the buildout is staggering. Current-year consensus capex estimates for the five hyperscalers have climbed from about $485 billion in January to around $730 billion in July, according to LSEG data. In the first quarter alone, the four largest spenders — Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta — invested a combined $129.8 billion, an 81% increase from the same period a year earlier and 9% above Q4 2025 levels.

According to UBS estimates cited by Reuters, hyperscaler capex will rise 76% this year to $673 billion, but growth is expected to moderate sharply — increasing by just 25% in 2027 and 6% in 2028. The spending covers data centers, servers, networking equipment and other cloud infrastructure that is overwhelmingly driven by AI demand, executives have said.

There are some signs the spending is paying off. Microsoft has said its AI business has surpassed a $37 billion annual revenue run rate. Amazon reported 28% growth at its AWS cloud unit in Q1. Google Cloud sales surged a record 63% in the same quarter.

Oracle: The Canary in the Coal Mine

The sharpest warning sign has come from Oracle. The company's shares have lost 36% this year as its free cash flow turned negative. Its capex as a percentage of operating cash flow rose from 47% in fiscal 2022 to 174% for fiscal 2026, which ended in May, according to LSEG data. Oracle spent $55.7 billion in its most recent fiscal year against just $32 billion in operating cash flow, and plans to raise $45 billion to $50 billion through debt and equity to fund further cloud infrastructure expansion.

Microsoft has also seen the pressure. The company reported $35.8 billion in operating cash flow in its fiscal second quarter alongside $37.5 billion in capital expenditures, including finance leases — meaning it spent more than it generated. Amazon's trailing 12-month free cash flow cratered to $1.2 billion despite a 30% rise in operating cash flow to $148.5 billion.

"Earnings growth may not be enough to justify investment if capex is depleting cash. Companies exist to make money, not spend money."

— David Russell, Global Head of Market Strategy, TradeStation

Earnings Season as Judgment Day

Alphabet reports Q2 earnings on Wednesday, with analysts expecting revenue to rise over 21% to $117 billion and adjusted earnings per share to increase 26% to $2.91, according to Koyfin estimates. Microsoft, Amazon and Meta follow next week. Nearly one-fifth of the S&P 500 by market value reports this week.

For investors, the questions have shifted. During the early phase of the AI boom, companies were rewarded for announcing larger spending plans — capex was treated as ambition, and ambition was a substitute for earnings. That equation has become less generous. Over the past year, all hyperscalers except Alphabet have trailed the S&P 500.

The Bank for International Settlements warned in a June report that a scaling back of AI capex could throw the global financial system into disorder, while Barron's noted that a "spending war" among the richest companies has caused prices of previously commoditized components like semiconductors and memory to surge.

What It Means for Diaspora Investors

The stakes extend well beyond Wall Street. Tech stocks dominate many Indian diaspora investment portfolios, and the sector is the largest employer of H-1B visa holders. Any sustained pullback in Big Tech spending or valuations could ripple through to hiring plans at companies where Indian-origin professionals hold a significant share of technical and leadership roles.

Meanwhile, the AI capex cycle is reshaping India's own tech landscape. Indian IT services firms including TCS, Infosys and Wipro have positioned themselves as key beneficiaries of enterprise AI adoption, and a slowdown in hyperscaler spending could dampen demand for the consulting and implementation work that has been a bright spot in recent quarters.

Looking Ahead

The coming weeks will test whether the AI investment thesis can survive contact with the balance sheet. Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta still generated enough free cash flow to cover dividends and buybacks in their latest fiscal years, according to SEC filings — but those shareholder returns could be at risk if spending stays elevated and AI monetization takes longer than expected.

"Over the next two to three years, companies need to show that AI is driving incremental revenue, expanding margins and improving cash flow," said Freddy Lavric, senior trader at Winthrop Capital Management. "If those financial benefits aren't becoming evident by then, the market will start questioning whether the investment cycle has gone too far."
